newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to seek waiver of diplomat's immunity.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to seek waiver of diplomat's immunity.

text.p: The U.S. State Department on Wednesday said it would ask the Georgian government to waive the immunity of a diplomat involved in a fatal five-vehicle crash once it received a police report on the case.

State Department spokeswoman Elaine McDevitt said the department notified the Georgian embassy of its decision after receiving a letter from the U.S. attorney's office which cited sufficient evidence to prosecute the diplomat.

Kevin Ohlson, spokesman for the U.S. attorney's office in Washington, said Gueorgui Makharadze, 35, could face charges ranging from negligent homicide to second degree murder, which carries a sentence of 20 years to life, if the Georgian government agreed to waive his immunity.
A 16-year-old American girl, Joviane Waltrick of Kensington, Maryland, died in the crash.
However officials do not expect Tbilisi to comply with the request, once it is formally made, in which case U.S. officials will press for Makharadze's withdrawal.
"We have notified that State Department that we believe we have a prosecutable case if diplomatic immunity is waived," Ohlson told Reuters late on Wednesday.

He said a preliminary investigation revealed "sufficient evidence that a criminal act was committed," noting that Makharadze appeared to have been speeding when the accident occurred and may have been under the influence of alcohol.

The case has caused an outcry in Washington over the whole concept of diplomatic immunity. Republican Senator Judd Gregg of New Hampshire on Monday urged President Bill Clinton to withhold aid to Georgia until it waived Makharadze's immunity.

The Georgian embassy on Tuesday issued a fresh statement of regret over the involvement of its diplomat in the accident, which has already prompted President Eduard Shevardnadze to send condolences to the Waltrick family.
"The Georgian government is fully cooperating with American authorities in this matter," it said in a statement issued through the Washington law firm of Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher and Flom.
But it said the embassy would have no further comment until investigations were completed.
The attorney representing Makharadze was not available for comment on Wednesday evening.
Ohlson said a final decision on which charges to bring against Makharadze would be made by a grand juury once the attorney's office had completed its investigation.
Ohlson also had no further comment on whether Makharadze had been drinking, saying only that "alcohol may have been involved."
